title: Eighteen NOAA hurricane outlooks permit zero joint range coverage under a count-order support model
abstract: We tested whether all probability summaries in 18 NOAA seasonal hurricane outlooks from 2021 to 2026 can hold in one distribution. We kept the four 70% range probabilities, season-type probabilities, ordered storm counts, and the stated season-type rules. Every outlook was feasible. For each, explicit distributions gave either zero or 70% probability that all four ranges hold together. Mixtures give every value between them. Thus the season-type statements and count order did not tighten the generic joint probability bounds. This is not a measured forecast failure, and NOAA does not promise 70% joint coverage. An at-least-70% reading still gave a zero lower bound. Equal 15% tails were impossible in two outlooks with a range starting at zero; the other 16 still allowed zero joint coverage. We provide original code, aggregate bounds, synthetic endpoint distributions, and independent exact-arithmetic checks of 104 distributions. The sharp bounds apply to a stated support model, not full hurricane physics. Inputs are inherited transcriptions; no new outcomes or physical error sources are tested.

display.caption: Sharp joint coverage bounds under the stated count-order support model. Blue segments use 70% per range. Orange segments add equal 15% lower tails, where feasible. No observed joint failure rate is estimated.

citations.reason: Verified source of outlook transcriptions; motivates the separate joint consistency question.
Count model scope audit motivates a distribution-free support test.
Prior linear programming method for sharp probability bounds; no novelty claimed for that general method.
